title: Constructive Partitioning Using Maximum Element Separation
approach_explanation: The problem requires partitioning an array $a$ into two non-empty arrays $b$ and $c$ such that no element in $c$ divides any element in $b$. A simple and effective strategy is to first sort or identify the maximum elements in the array $a$. If all elements in $a$ are identical, no such partition can exist because any element chosen from $c$ would divide any element in $b$, so we output -1. Otherwise, we can place all occurrences of the maximum element into array $c$ and all other elements into array $b$. Since all elements in $b$ are strictly smaller than the elements in $c$ (or at least not equal to the maximum), no element in $c$ can divide any element in $b$ (as a smaller number cannot be a multiple of a larger number, and if they are equal, they would be in $c$).

code_breakdown.explanation: Defines `print_vector` to print elements of a vector separated by spaces and `check_all_equal_elements` to check whether all elements in the array are identical.

code_breakdown.section_title: Test Case Reading and Maximum Tracking
code_breakdown.explanation: Reads the number of test cases $t$, and for each test case reads the size $n$ and elements into array $a$ while concurrently tracking the maximum value (`max`).
Checks if all elements in array $a$ are equal using `check_all_equal_elements(a)`. If they are, it prints `-1` because no valid partition can satisfy the condition.

Iterates through array $a$, placing all elements equal to `max` into array $c$, and all other elements into array $b$. This guarantees that array $b$ and array $c$ are both non-empty and satisfy the divisibility condition.
Prints the sizes of arrays $b$ and $c$, followed by their contents using the helper function `print_vector`.

complexity_analysis.time_justification: Finding the maximum element and checking if all elements are equal each take a single pass through the array of size $n$. Partitioning takes another pass. Thus, for each test case, the time complexity is linear in $n$. Summing over $t$ test cases, total time complexity is $O(\sum n)$, which easily passes within the 1-second limit for $n \le 100$ and $t \le 500$.
complexity_analysis.space_justification: Vectors $a$, $b$, and $c$ store up to $n$ integers combined, requiring linear extra space per test case.

strengths: Simple and intuitive logic based on isolating the maximum element.
Clear modularization with helper functions for printing and equality checking.
edge_cases_handled: Handles arrays with all identical elements by correctly outputting -1.
best_practices_feedback: Avoid naming variables `max` as it shadows the standard library function `std::max`, which can lead to hard-to-debug compilation issues in larger scopes.
Use `std::vector::size()` type `size_t` or cast appropriately to avoid signed/unsigned comparison warnings.
Include fast I/O (`ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(NULL);`) for competitive programming safety.

optimization_and_alternatives.tradeoffs: Sorting the array allows grouping the smallest elements together or finding the suffix of maximum elements easily. Though slightly slower than $O(n)$ due to sorting, it offers great flexibility for variants of this problem.
